docs.title: docker-postgres-snapshot Documentation
docs.text:
A Docker image that wraps pg_dump and rsnapshot to provide a drop-in solution for periodic snapshots of PostgreSQL databases with automated rotation and retention.

The primary goals of docker-postgres-snapshot are reliability, simplicity, and ease of use. It is the PostgreSQL counterpart of docker-mariadb-snapshot.

Your Responsibility

Please review the Important Considerations document. This package has not been reviewed for all possible use cases and environments. It should be considered an example, rather than a production-ready tool. Please ensure that you audit this package and how you deploy it against your specific environment and requirements.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: The image carries the PostgreSQL 17 and 18 clients and dumps each server with the client of its own major version. See Compatibility.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When run with the lowest retained frequency argument (normally hourly), the image:

  1. Connects to your PostgreSQL server and picks the pg_dump matching the server's major version
  2. Selects databases from an explicit list or by discovery
  3. Applies structure-only table rules if configured
  4. Dumps each database to a plain SQL file in the container's /tmp, and compresses it only after pg_dump has finished
  5. Optionally dumps roles and tablespaces (globals.sql.gz) and a single cluster-wide file
  6. Writes a snapshot-metadata.json file with timing, versions and configuration
  7. Rotates snapshots according to retention policies into hourly.0/, hourly.1/, and so on

When run with a higher level (daily, weekly, monthly), it only promotes the oldest snapshot of the level below; see Understanding the rsnapshot Configuration. If any dump fails, the run exits non-zero and leaves the existing snapshots untouched; see Important Considerations.

docs.title: Dumping
docs.text:
The image carries the PostgreSQL 17 and 18 clients and dumps each server with the client of the same major version, so the dump contains nothing the server's own version could not have produced. The test suite runs every scenario against both.

A server of any other major version is dumped with the newest client, which logs a warning. pg_dump supports servers back to 9.2, so older servers still work; a server newer than every installed client is refused by pg_dump itself. The client actually used is recorded in snapshot-metadata.json.

To support another major version, add its postgresqlNN-client package to the Dockerfile and its server to the test suite.

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
A dump restores into a server of the same major version, which is the case the tests prove. Restoring into a newer major version is the supported PostgreSQL upgrade path. Restoring into an older one is not supported by PostgreSQL and may fail on statements the older server does not know.

Dumps start with \restrict, which psql gained in the August 2025 minor releases (17.6, 16.10, 15.14, 14.19, 13.22). Restore with a psql at least that recent; see Restoring Snapshots.

docs.title: Snapshot Configuration
docs.text: All configuration options are set via environment variables within the running container.

docs.title: rsnapshot Retention Settings
docs.text:
Control how many snapshots rsnapshot retains (follows rsnapshot retention models). A value of 0 removes the level entirely; every level that you do not schedule must be 0. See Understanding the rsnapshot Configuration.

Variable Description Default RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY Number of hourly snapshots to retain 8 RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_DAILY Number of daily snapshots to retain 7 RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_WEEKLY Number of weekly snapshots to retain 4 RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_MONTHLY Number of monthly snapshots to retain 6

docs.title: General Settings
docs.text:
Variable Description Default GZIP_COMPRESSION_LEVEL Level of gzip compression (1-9) 6 DB_DUMP_LOCATION Directory where snapshots are stored /data DB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT How long pg_dump waits for its shared table locks before failing, in any format SET statement_timeout accepts 10min

Each dump is written uncompressed to the container's /tmp and compressed only after pg_dump has exited, so the database's snapshot and locks are released before compression starts. The container's /tmp must therefore hold the largest uncompressed dump.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Connection Parameters
docs.text: Variable Description Default DB_HOSTNAME Hostname or IP address of the server localhost DB_PORT Port of the server 5432 DB_USER_NAME Role to connect as postgres DB_USER_PASSWORD Password for that role (empty) DB_MAINTENANCE_DATABASE Database used for discovery, version checks and pg_dumpall postgres DB_SSLMODE libpq sslmode prefer DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT Seconds to wait for a connection 30

docs.title: Required Privileges
docs.text:
• Database dumps need read access to everything dumped. On PostgreSQL 14 and newer, a role with the predefined pg_read_all_data role is enough.
  • DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS and DB_SNAPSHOT_COMBINED read pg_authid and need a superuser. With any other role, leave both off: a dump that fails every night freezes the snapshots at the last good run, as described in Important Considerations.

docs.title: Client Selection
docs.text: The image carries the PostgreSQL 17 and 18 clients. Each run reads the server's version and uses the pg_dump of the same major version, so a dump restores into the same major version without features the server does not have. For any other server version it uses the newest client and logs a warning; a newer pg_dump can dump an older server. The client used is recorded in snapshot-metadata.json.

docs.title: Mode 1: Explicit List
docs.text: Variable Description Example DB_DATABASES Comma-separated list of databases to snapshot db1,db2,db3

docs.title: Mode 2: Discovery
docs.text:
Discover and snapshot every database that accepts connections and is not a template, including postgres.

Variable Description Default DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES Set to true or 1 to enable discovery (disabled) DB_EXCLUDE_DATABASES Comma-separated database names to skip, matched exactly (empty) DB_SNAPSHOT_COMBINED Also write ALL_DATABASES.gz with pg_dumpall (disabled)

If both are set, DB_DATABASES wins.

docs.title: Structure-Only Tables
docs.text:
Tables whose data is not worth keeping (caches, sessions) can be dumped as structure only.

Variable Description Example DB_STRUCT_TABLES Comma-separated table name patterns for every database cache_*,sessions DB_STRUCT_TABLES_<NORMALIZED_DB_NAME> Patterns for one database, replacing the global list cache_*,watchdog

Pattern matching:

  • * matches any characters; patterns are matched with SQL LIKE against table names in every schema except pg_catalog and information_schema, so _ matches any single character.
  • Matching is case-sensitive and exact otherwise; a pattern that matches nothing is ignored.
  • The table's definition, indexes and constraints are still dumped; only its rows are left out.

<NORMALIZED_DB_NAME> is the database name in upper case with every character other than letters, digits and _ replaced by _:

Database Name Environment Variable myapp DB_STRUCT_TABLES_MYAPP my-app DB_STRUCT_TABLES_MY_APP Mixed-Case DB_STRUCT_TABLES_MIXED_CASE

docs.title: Globals Snapshot
docs.text:
Variable Description Default DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS Set to true or 1 to write globals.sql.gz with pg_dumpall --globals-only (disabled)

globals.sql.gz holds roles with their password hashes, role memberships and settings, and tablespaces. Per-database dumps reference roles as owners and grantees, so restoring a database onto a new server needs the globals first. See Restoring Snapshots.

docs.title: Within a Database
docs.text: pg_dump reads the whole database inside one transaction at the REPEATABLE READ isolation level, so every table in a dump reflects the same moment. Relationships between tables are intact, and this holds for every table regardless of how it is stored. Reads and writes continue while the dump runs.

docs.title: Across Databases
docs.text: Each database is dumped separately, one after another, so two databases from the same run reflect different moments. ALL_DATABASES.gz is built the same way by pg_dumpall. If an application keeps related data in more than one database, a restore of that run can pair data that never coexisted.

docs.title: Globals
docs.text: globals.sql.gz is taken after the database dumps. A role created or dropped while the run was in progress may be missing from it or present without objects.

docs.title: Not Used
docs.text: --serializable-deferrable is not used. It guarantees a dump that is consistent with every serializable transaction, at the cost of waiting for a safe moment to start, and matters only for applications that rely on SERIALIZABLE isolation. See the pg_dump documentation.

docs.title: Drop-In Example
docs.text:
services:
  postgres:
    [...]

  postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
    restart: "no"
    environment:
      DB_HOSTNAME: postgres
      DB_USER_NAME: postgres
      DB_USER_PASSWORD: changeme
      DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES: "true"
      DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS: "true"
      RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY: 24
      RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_DAILY: 14
      RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_WEEKLY: 8
      RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_MONTHLY: 12
    volumes:
      - ./snapshots:/data
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

docs.title: Specific Databases
docs.text:
postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
    restart: "no"

      DB_HOSTNAME: postgres
      DB_USER_NAME: postgres
      DB_USER_PASSWORD: changeme
      DB_DATABASES: "app1,app2,app3"
      DB_STRUCT_TABLES: "cache_*,sessions"
    volumes:
      - ./snapshots:/data

docs.title: Discovery With Exclusions
docs.text:
postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
    restart: "no"
    environment:
      DB_HOSTNAME: postgres
      DB_USER_NAME: postgres
      DB_USER_PASSWORD: changeme
      DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES: "true"
      DB_EXCLUDE_DATABASES: "scratch,reporting_copy"
    volumes:
      - ./snapshots:/data

docs.title: Structure-Only Tables Per Database
docs.text:
postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
    restart: "no"
    environment:
      DB_HOSTNAME: postgres
      DB_USER_NAME: postgres
      DB_USER_PASSWORD: changeme
      DB_DATABASES: "app1,app2"
      DB_STRUCT_TABLES_APP1: "cache_*,sessions,watchdog"
      DB_STRUCT_TABLES_APP2: "temp_*,cache"
    volumes:
      - ./snapshots:/data

docs.title: Running Snapshots
docs.text:
docker compose run --rm <service-name> <frequency>

Where <frequency> is one of hourly, daily, weekly or monthly.

docs.title: Important Considerations
docs.text:
Please Read

These considerations help you judge whether docker-postgres-snapshot suits your environment.

docker-postgres-snapshot takes logical dumps. It is not point-in-time recovery: anything written after the last successful dump is not in any snapshot. If you need recovery to an arbitrary moment, use continuous archiving of the write-ahead log instead of, or as well as, this image.

docs.title: Testing Snapshot Restorations
docs.text: Test a restore immediately after the first snapshots exist, in a non-production environment, following Restoring Snapshots as if the original were gone. Repeat it periodically.

docs.title: Sensitive Data
docs.text: Snapshots are plain SQL and contain everything in the database, including role password hashes in globals.sql.gz. The image writes every file with mode 0600. Restrict access to wherever the snapshots are stored.

docs.title: Failed Runs Exit Non-Zero and Change Nothing
docs.text:
If any part of a run fails (one database, the globals, or the combined file), the image exits with a non-zero status. rsnapshot rolls the run back, discarding the dumps that did succeed, and the image skips rotation. The snapshots on disk are exactly as they were before the run. See Understanding the rsnapshot Configuration.

The consequence: a failure that repeats every run freezes your snapshots at the last good one, while each run reports failure. For example, enabling DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS with a role that is not a superuser fails every night. Watch the exit status of every run, and alert when the newest successful snapshot is older than you expect.

docs.title: Container Restart Policies
docs.text: Do not let the orchestrator retry a failed run automatically; a retry repeats the same failure and adds load to the server.

docs.title: docker-compose
docs.text:
service:
    [...]
    restart: "no"

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
restartPolicy: Never
    backoffLimit: 0
    activeDeadlineSeconds: 7200

With concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, a run that hangs blocks every later run until it ends; activeDeadlineSeconds makes sure it does.

docs.title: Locks Taken During a Dump
docs.text: pg_dump takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on every table it dumps and holds it for the whole dump. That does not block reads or writes, but it blocks schema changes (for example, a migration's ALTER TABLE), and statements queued behind a waiting schema change wait too. DB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT makes the dump give up if it cannot get its locks, instead of queueing behind a schema change already in progress. Schedule dumps away from deployments.

docs.title: Dump Options
docs.text:
Each database is dumped with:

    --format=plain
    --clean
    --if-exists
    --lock-wait-timeout=${DB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT}
    --exclude-table-data=<each structure-only table>

The dump is written uncompressed to the container's /tmp, then compressed with gzip. It is never piped straight into the compressor, so the server's snapshot and locks are released as soon as the dump ends.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text: Each database is captured as of a single moment. Different databases are captured at different moments. See Snapshot Consistency.

docs.title: Kubernetes Deployment
docs.text:
Schedule snapshots with one CronJob per retention level. Each CronJob runs the image with its level as the only argument.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: postgres-snapshot-config
data:
  DB_HOSTNAME: "postgres.default.svc.cluster.local"
  DB_PORT: "5432"
  DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES: "true"
  DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS: "true"
  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY: "0"
  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_DAILY: "7"
  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_WEEKLY: "4"
  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_MONTHLY: "12"

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Reference the same Secret the database itself uses, so there is one source for the password:

env:
  - name: DB_USER_NAME
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: myapp
        key: postgres-user
  - name: DB_USER_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: myapp
        key: postgres-password

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-snapshot-storage
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi

Use storage that is not on the database's own node or disk; a snapshot that shares the database's failure domain does not protect against losing it.

docs.title: CronJob
docs.text:
The daily level, which is the lowest retained level in the configuration above and so the only one that dumps:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: postgres-snapshot-daily
spec:
  schedule: "30 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 480
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 0
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 7200
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 604800
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: postgres-snapshot
              image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
              args: ["daily"]
              envFrom:
                - configMapRef:
                    name: postgres-snapshot-config
              env:
                - name: DB_USER_NAME
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef: {name: myapp, key: postgres-user}
                - name: DB_USER_PASSWORD
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef: {name: myapp, key: postgres-password}
              volumeMounts:
                - name: snapshot-storage
                  mountPath: /data
          volumes:
            - name: snapshot-storage
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: postgres-snapshot-storage

Create weekly ("30 5 * * 0") and monthly ("30 7 1 * *") CronJobs the same way, changing only the name, schedule and argument. Schedule them after the daily run so the two never overlap: rsnapshot's lock file lives inside each container and does not protect one Job from another.

Notes on the Job settings:

  • restartPolicy: Never with backoffLimit: 0 keeps a failed run from retrying into the same failure. See Important Considerations.
  • concurrencyPolicy: Forbid together with activeDeadlineSeconds keeps one hung run from blocking every later one forever: the deadline ends it and the next schedule runs.

docs.title: Snapshot Metadata
docs.text:
Each run that dumps writes a snapshot-metadata.json file beside the dumps, and rsnapshot rotates it with them. A promoted weekly or monthly snapshot keeps the metadata of the run that created it, so its frequency is the lowest level's (for example daily).

Contents:

  • Snapshot information: start time, end time, duration in seconds, and the level that ran
  • Database server: PostgreSQL, its version, and the full version() string
  • Client information: the path and version of the pg_dump used, which shows the major version selected
  • Configuration: the settings that shaped the snapshot, without credentials

Example: 

{
  "snapshot_info": {
    "start_time": "2026-10-30T19:03:31Z",
    "end_time": "2026-10-30T19:03:31Z",
    "duration_seconds": 0,
    "frequency": "hourly"
  },
  "database_server": {
    "type": "PostgreSQL",
    "version": "18.6",
    "version_string": "PostgreSQL 18.6 on x86_64-pc-linux-musl, compiled by gcc (Alpine 15.2.0) 15.2.0, 64-bit"
  },
  "client_info": {
    "pg_dump_path": "/usr/libexec/postgresql18/pg_dump",
    "pg_dump_version": "pg_dump (PostgreSQL) 18.6"
  },
  "configuration": {
    "DB_HOSTNAME": "pg18",
    "DB_PORT": "5432",
    "DB_DATABASES": "app1,app2,app3",
    "DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES": "",
    "DB_SNAPSHOT_COMBINED": "",
    "DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS": "true",
    "DB_EXCLUDE_DATABASES": "",
    "DB_STRUCT_TABLES": "cache_*,sessions",
    "DB_SSLMODE": "prefer",
    "DB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT": "10min",
    "RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY": "8",
    "RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_DAILY": "7",
    "RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_WEEKLY": "4",
    "RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_MONTHLY": "6",
    "GZIP_COMPRESSION_LEVEL": "6"
  }
}

Security note: the file never contains DB_USER_NAME or DB_USER_PASSWORD.

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text:
Get up and running with docker-postgres-snapshot in 5 minutes.

Your Responsibility

Please review the Important Considerations document. This package has not been reviewed for all possible use cases and environments. It should be considered an example, rather than a production-ready tool. Please ensure that you audit this package and how you deploy it against your specific environment and requirements.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
docker-postgres-snapshot accepts one argument to specify the snapshot frequency:

  • hourly - Performs an hourly snapshot
  • daily - Performs a daily snapshot
  • weekly - Performs a weekly snapshot
  • monthly - Performs a monthly snapshot

These are labels passed to rsnapshot, which handles snapshot rotation based on your retention configuration. Only the lowest retained level (hourly by default) dumps the databases; higher levels promote the oldest snapshot of the level below. If you do not schedule hourly, set RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY=0. See Understanding the rsnapshot Configuration.

docs.title: Docker Run Example
docs.text:
A minimal example snapshotting one database:

docker run --rm \
  -e DB_HOSTNAME=postgres.example.com \
  -e DB_PORT=5432 \
  -e DB_USER_NAME=postgres \
  -e DB_USER_PASSWORD=secure_password \
  -e DB_DATABASES=myapp \
  -v /path/to/snapshots:/data \
  ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x hourly

This creates a snapshot in /path/to/snapshots/hourly.0/postgres/myapp.gz.

docs.title: Docker Compose Quick Example
docs.text:
Create a docker-compose.yml:

services:
  postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
    restart: "no"
    environment:
      DB_HOSTNAME: postgres
      DB_USER_NAME: postgres
      DB_USER_PASSWORD: changeme
      DB_SNAPSHOT_ALL_DATABASES: "true"
      DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS: "true"
    volumes:
      - ./snapshots:/data

Run a snapshot:

docker compose run --rm postgres-snapshot hourly

docs.title: Scheduling with Cron
docs.text:
To run automated snapshots, add to your crontab:

# Hourly snapshots at minute 0
0 * * * * cd /path/to/compose && docker compose run --rm postgres-snapshot hourly

# Daily snapshots at 2am
0 2 * * * cd /path/to/compose && docker compose run --rm postgres-snapshot daily

# Weekly snapshots on Sunday at 3am
0 3 * * 0 cd /path/to/compose && docker compose run --rm postgres-snapshot weekly

# Monthly snapshots on the 1st at 4am
0 4 1 * * cd /path/to/compose && docker compose run --rm postgres-snapshot monthly

docs.title: Understanding Snapshot Output
docs.text:
/data/
├── .sync/          # The last dump taken by the lowest level
├── hourly.0/       # Most recent hourly snapshot
│   └── postgres/
│       ├── myapp.gz
│       ├── globals.sql.gz
│       └── snapshot-metadata.json
├── hourly.1/       # Previous hourly snapshot
├── daily.0/        # Most recent daily snapshot
└── weekly.0/       # Most recent weekly snapshot

The .0 directories contain the newest snapshots. Older snapshots are rotated to .1, .2, and so on, according to your retention policy. Unchanged files are hard links between generations, so they take no extra space.

docs.title: Restoring Snapshots
docs.text:
Test Restorations First

Restore a snapshot into a scratch server as soon as the first one exists, and periodically after that. Each procedure on this page is exercised by the image's own test suite against PostgreSQL 17 and 18.

docs.title: What a Snapshot Contains
docs.text:
• <database>.gz - A plain SQL dump of one database: schemas, tables, data, indexes, constraints, functions, triggers, extensions, owners and privileges. It starts with DROP ... IF EXISTS for every object, and it does not create the database itself.
  • globals.sql.gz - Roles, their password hashes, memberships and settings, and tablespaces (if DB_SNAPSHOT_GLOBALS was on).
  • ALL_DATABASES.gz - Everything above in one pg_dumpall file (if DB_SNAPSHOT_COMBINED was on).
  • snapshot-metadata.json - When the dump ran, the server and client versions, and the configuration.

Structure-only tables are restored empty.

docs.title: Use a Matching psql
docs.text:
Restore with a psql of the dump's major version (see pg_dump_version in the metadata) or newer. Dumps start with a \restrict line, a protection added in the August 2025 minor releases (17.6, 16.10, 15.14, 14.19, 13.22); an older psql is expected to reject it. The image itself carries current clients:

docker run --rm -i --entrypoint /usr/libexec/postgresql18/psql \
  ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x --version

docs.title: Disaster Recovery Onto an Empty Server
docs.text:
Start an empty server of the same major version, created with the same superuser name as the original. Then:

  1. Globals first. Owners and grants in the database dumps refer to these roles.

    gunzip -c globals.sql.gz | psql -h NEWHOST -U postgres -d postgres

    Expect exactly one error, role "postgres" already exists, for the superuser the new server was created with. Any other error needs attention before continuing.

  2. Create each database with its original owner.

    psql -h NEWHOST -U postgres -d postgres -c 'CREATE DATABASE myapp OWNER myapp_owner'

  3. Restore each dump, stopping at the first error.

    gunzip -c myapp.gz | psql -h NEWHOST -U postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d myapp

Restore as a superuser: dumps set owners and create extensions.

docs.title: Restoring Into an Existing Database
docs.text:
The dumps drop and recreate every object they contain, so the same command restores over an existing database:

gunzip -c myapp.gz | psql -h HOST -U postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d myapp

Objects in the database that are not in the dump are left in place. Stop the application first; the restore takes locks and replaces tables underneath it.

docs.title: Restoring the Combined File
docs.text:
ALL_DATABASES.gz drops and recreates every role and database it contains:

gunzip -c ALL_DATABASES.gz | psql -h HOST -U postgres -d postgres

It cannot drop a database that has open connections, or the role you are connected as, so use it on an empty or isolated server.

docs.title: Examining Snapshots
docs.text:
# View the SQL without running it
gunzip -c myapp.gz | less

# Check the file is intact
gunzip -t myapp.gz && echo "File is valid"

# Review metadata
jq . snapshot-metadata.json

docs.title: 'Frequency' Labels
docs.text:
The environment variable names and rsnapshot configuration use the terms hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly for different retention levels:

retain  hourly  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY
retain  daily   RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_DAILY
retain  weekly  RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_WEEKLY
retain  monthly RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_MONTHLY

rsnapshot does not understand time. These are labels for separate retention groups. How often each level runs is decided only by how often you run the image with that argument (for example, from cron).

docs.title: Snapshot Rotation
docs.text:
The image uses rsnapshot's standard rotation with sync_first 1. Only the lowest retained level (the first retain line left in the configuration, normally hourly, or daily when RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY is 0) dumps the live databases. Every higher level promotes the oldest snapshot of the level below it and does not connect to the database at all.

With RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY=0 and the default daily, weekly and monthly retention, running the image with:

  • daily dumps into .sync, rotates the daily set (daily.5 → daily.6, ..., daily.0 → daily.1), and makes the new dump daily.0.
  • weekly rotates the weekly set and moves the oldest daily (daily.6) to weekly.0. Nothing is dumped. Until seven dailies exist there is nothing to promote, and rsnapshot logs daily.6 not present (yet), nothing to copy.
  • monthly does the same with the oldest weekly (weekly.3).

A weekly or monthly snapshot is therefore the dump taken by the lowest level, and its snapshot-metadata.json records that original run, including "frequency": "daily".

Every level you schedule must have a non-zero retention, and the lowest level must run often enough to feed the levels above it. A level that is retained but never run becomes the lowest level, and then nothing is ever promoted. Set its retention to 0.

docs.title: Failed Runs
docs.text:
rsnapshot runs the dump script with its working directory in <snapshot_root>/tmp, then copies the results into .sync. When the script exits non-zero, rsnapshot rolls .sync back to the newest snapshot of the lowest level, discarding every file from that run, including the databases that did dump successfully.

The image then stops without rotating and exits with rsnapshot's non-zero status. Rotating at that point would only create a copy of the previous snapshot and push the oldest distinct one out of retention. The result of a failed run is that nothing changes on disk and the orchestrator sees a failure.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
The testing/ directory holds a self-contained suite for the image. It needs Docker with Compose v2, and python3 for the JSON check.

cd testing
./run-tests.sh

If containers cannot resolve the Alpine package mirrors during the build (some VPNs cause this), build on the host network:

BUILD_NETWORK=host ./run-tests.sh

The runner:

  1. Removes old containers and snapshots
  2. Builds the image as postgres-snapshot:test
  3. Starts PostgreSQL 17 and 18 seeded from init-db.sql, plus an empty server of each version for restores
  4. Runs every scenario and check
  5. Removes the containers

docs.title: What the Tests Cover
docs.text: Area What is checked Explicit list Every database dumped on 17 and 18, complete and valid gzip Client selection The metadata names the client of the server's own major version Structure-only tables Global and per-database patterns keep the table definition and drop its rows; a quoted table name with a space in a mixed-case database Discovery Includes postgres and a mixed-case database, honours DB_EXCLUDE_DATABASES Combined ALL_DATABASES.gz is a complete pg_dumpall dump with roles, without excluded databases Globals globals.sql.gz contains the non-superuser role Permissions Every snapshot file has mode 0600 Disaster recovery Globals, then each database, into an empty server of the same major; row counts, a table owned by a non-superuser role, and data from the pgcrypto extension In-place restore The same dumps restored again over the restored databases Rotation Only the lowest level dumps; weekly promotes the oldest daily Failure A missing database makes the run exit non-zero, rsnapshot rolls back, nothing rotates, and no password appears in the log Lock wait A table held in ACCESS EXCLUSIVE mode makes the dump fail within DB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT, not after the lock is released

docs.title: Inspecting Snapshots
docs.text:
Snapshot files are written by root with mode 0600. The runner copies them into testing/view/, owned by you, after every run:

gunzip -c testing/view/multiple-18/hourly.0/postgres/app1.gz | less

docs.title: Running One Scenario
docs.text:
cd testing
docker build -t postgres-snapshot:test ..
docker compose up -d --wait pg18
docker compose run --rm snapshot-multiple-18 hourly

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
cd testing
docker compose down -v
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/w" alpine:3.24 rm -rf /w/snapshots /w/view

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the suite on every push and pull request, then builds and pushes the image.

docs.title: Reporting Security Issues
docs.text:
Do NOT file public GitHub issues for security vulnerabilities.

To report a security vulnerability, please contact the project maintainers directly:

  1. Preferred: Use GitHub Security Advisories to privately report vulnerabilities
  2. Alternative: Contact the repository owner directly through GitHub

docs.title: What to Include
docs.text:
When reporting a vulnerability, please provide:

  • Description of the vulnerability
  • Steps to reproduce
  • Potential impact
  • Suggested fix (if available)

docs.title: Response Time
docs.text: We aim to respond to security reports within 72 hours and will work with you to address the issue promptly.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text: See Important Considerations for general security guidance when using this project.

docs.title: Documentation Style Guide
docs.text: This brief style guide ensures consistency across the docker-postgres-snapshot documentation.

docs.title: Product Naming
docs.text:
Canonical Name: docker-postgres-snapshot

Use this exact form in all documentation.

docs.title: Front Matter
docs.text:
All .md files must include complete YAML front matter:

---
title: Page Title
description: One-sentence summary of the page content
audience: users|operators|developers
doc_type: tutorial|howto|explanation|reference|guide|landing|quickstart
tags: [keyword1, keyword2, keyword3]
lastReviewed: YYYY-MM-DD
version: 1.x
---

Required fields:

  • title: Descriptive page title
  • description: Brief one-sentence summary
  • audience: Target reader (users, operators, or developers)
  • doc_type: Documentation type following Diátaxis framework
  • tags: Array of relevant keywords
  • lastReviewed: ISO date of last review
  • version: Product version (currently 1.x)

docs.title: Headings
docs.text:
Capitalization: Use sentence case with key terms capitalized

Examples:

  • ✓ ## Docker Compose Examples
  • ✓ ## Structure-Only Tables
  • ✓ ## PostgreSQL Connection Parameters
  • ✗ ## docker compose examples (too lowercase)
  • ✗ ## DOCKER COMPOSE EXAMPLES (too uppercase)

Hierarchy: Do not skip heading levels (h2 → h4)

docs.title: Code Blocks
docs.text:
Always specify the language for syntax highlighting:

```bash
docker run --rm ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x daily
```

```yaml
services:
  postgres-snapshot:
    image: ghcr.io/jacobsanford/postgres-snapshot:1.x
```

```json
{
  "snapshot_time": "2025-11-16T12:00:00Z"
}
```

Supported languages: bash, yaml, json, sql, text

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
External links: Always use {target="_blank"} to open in new tabs

[Docker](https://www.docker.com){target="_blank"}
[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org){target="_blank"}

Internal links: Use relative paths without {target="_blank"}

[Configuration Reference](configuration.md)
[Quick Start](quickstart.md)

Link text: Use descriptive text, avoid "click here" or bare URLs

  • ✓ See the [Configuration Reference](configuration.md) for details
  • ✗ Click [here](configuration.md) for more information

docs.title: Inline Code
docs.text:
Use backticks for:

  • File paths: `/data`, `snapshot.sh`
  • Environment variables: `DB_HOSTNAME`, `RSNAPSHOT_RETAIN_HOURLY`
  • Commands: `docker compose run`
  • Code references: `pg_dump`, `rsnapshot`

docs.title: Admonitions
docs.text:
Use MkDocs admonitions for important information:

!!! warning "Your Responsibility"
    This package should be considered an example rather than production-ready.

!!! note "Tip"
    Higher compression levels reduce file size but increase CPU usage.

Common types: warning, note, tip, info

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Use pipe tables with header separators:

| Variable | Description | Default |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `DB_HOSTNAME` | Database server hostname | `localhost` |
| `DB_PORT` | Database server port | `3306` |

docs.title: Tone and Voice
docs.text:
Style: Professional, technical, directive

  • Use active voice: ✓ "Configure the database hostname" vs. ✗ "The database hostname should be configured"
  • Be direct and concise
  • Assume reader has Docker and database familiarity
  • Avoid excessive pleasantries or conversational asides

docs.title: File Organization
docs.text:
New pages: 1. Create the .md file in docs/ 2. Add complete front matter 3. Add to navigation in mkdocs.yml 4. Include cross-references to related pages

Images: - Store in docs/images/ - Optimize to <500 KB - Always include descriptive alt text
